note.explanation: A distance-time graph shows how distance changes with time. Its slope tells us the speed: a straight rising line means uniform speed, a curved line can show changing speed, and a horizontal line means the body is at rest.
examples: If a car travels 1.2 km each minute, its distance-time graph is a straight rising line.
If distance stays at 1.2 km as time passes, the graph is horizontal and the car is at rest.
note.simple: Look at how the graph changes as you move to the right. If distance rises evenly, speed is uniform. If distance does not change, the body is not moving.

written.text:
The figure given below shows the distance - time graph for the travel of a cyclist. Find the velocities for the segments a, b and c.

[FIGURE: Distance - time graph with vertical axis labelled “Distance → S (km)” and horizontal axis labelled “Time → t (min)”. The vertical scale is 0 to 2.0 in increments of 0.2; the horizontal scale is 0 to 20 in increments of 2. Segment a rises from (0, 0) to (6, 2.0), segment b is horizontal from (6, 2.0) to (10, 2.0), and segment c falls from (10, 2.0) to (20, 0).]
written.finalAnswer: a = 20 km h⁻¹; b = 0; c = −12 km h⁻¹

rubric.why: Velocity for each graph segment is found from its gradient.
rubric.description: Uses the gradient of a distance-time graph.
rubric.how: State or use velocity = change in distance/change in time.

rubric.why: The first segment has a positive gradient.
rubric.description: Finds the velocity for segment a.

rubric.why: The second segment is horizontal, so its gradient is zero.
rubric.description: Finds the velocity for segment b.
rubric.how: Use the unchanged distance from 6 to 10 min.

rubric.why: The final segment falls, so its gradient and velocity are negative.
rubric.description: Finds the velocity for segment c.

modelAnswer: Velocity = gradient of the distance-time graph = change in distance/change in time.
For segment a: velocity = (2.0 − 0) km/(6 − 0) min = 1/3 km min⁻¹ = 20 km h⁻¹.
For segment b: velocity = (2.0 − 2.0) km/(10 − 6) min = 0.
For segment c: velocity = (0 − 2.0) km/(20 − 10) min = −1/5 km min⁻¹ = −12 km h⁻¹.
Therefore, a = 20 km h⁻¹, b = 0, and c = −12 km h⁻¹.

written.text: What do gradients of distance-time graph and speed-time graph represent? Explain it by drawing diagrams.
written.finalAnswer: The gradient of a distance-time graph represents speed. The gradient of a speed-time graph represents acceleration.

rubric.how: Write change in distance/change in time.

rubric.how: Write change in speed/change in time.

modelAnswer: Gradient = change in vertical-axis quantity/change in horizontal-axis quantity.
For a distance-time graph, gradient = change in distance/change in time = speed.
For a speed-time graph, gradient = change in speed/change in time = acceleration.

example.question:
Let a car be moving in a straight line on a motorway. Suppose that we measure its distance from starting point after every one minute, and record it in the table given below:

Time t (min): 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5
Distance S (km): 0, 1.2, 2.4, 3.6, 4.8, 6.0

Draw a graph of the motion.
example.answer: The plotted points form a straight rising line, so the car moves with uniform speed.

explain.title: What a graph shows
explain.body: A graph is a pictorial diagram in the form of a straight line or a curve which shows the relationship between two physical quantities. Time is usually the independent quantity on the x-axis, and the dependent quantity is on the y-axis.

explain.title: Distance-time graph
explain.body: Distance-time graph shows the relation between distance S and time t taken by a moving body. A straight rising line shows uniform speed because the car covers equal distances in equal intervals of time.

explain.title: Curved distance-time graphs
explain.body: An upward-curving graph shows that speed is increasing. A graph that curves downwards and becomes flatter shows that the distance travelled in the same time interval is decreasing, so speed is decreasing.

explain.title: Horizontal distance-time graph
explain.body: If the graph is horizontal, distance does not change with time. The body is at rest.

mistakes: Putting time on the y-axis instead of the x-axis.
Forgetting to choose and label a suitable scale on both axes.
Treating every curved graph as uniform motion; a curved distance-time graph shows changing speed.
Calling a horizontal distance-time graph uniform motion instead of rest.
Leaving out units or the negative sign when calculating the gradient of a falling segment.
